--- Page 1 ---
Optimal Scheduling of Multi-Site AI Data Centers in Day-Ahead Markets
Xinyang Zhou and Guido Cavraro
National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO, USA; Email: xinyang.zhou@nlr.gov, guido.cavraro@nlr.gov
Abstract—AI data centers are among the fastest-growing loads
on the power grid, and their flexibility is increasingly sought
by grid operators. Using it requires a model that links what
an operator controls, namely GPU power caps, job timing
and job placement, to the power drawn at each site and the
electricity prices it faces. This paper develops such a framework
for a multi-site AI data-center fleet. It represents GPU power-
cap levels; deferrable jobs with deadlines and inference with
response-time headroom; and site facility power, and casts the
fleet schedule as a linear program solved on day-ahead prices.
A year-long simulation on 2025 California Independent System
Operator (CAISO) day-ahead prices in three data-center markets
demonstrates the framework. Coordinated scheduling lowers the
fleet’s energy cost by 6.3% at equal work. Four operating modes,
each adding one capability, split this saving into efficient GPU
operation that needs no price signal, price response in time, and
routing work between sites.
Index Terms—Data centers, demand flexibility, GPU power
capping, locational marginal price, linear programming.
I. INTRODUCTION
U.S. data centers used 4.7% of the nation’s electricity in
2024 and may use 9.5–15.3% by 2030 [1], driven mainly by
AI servers. About 100 GW of new large load could connect if
curtailed by about 0.5% of its maximum annual energy use [2].
Field tests have held a GPU cluster 25% below baseline for
three hours during a grid peak [3] and, in a later London trial,
cut a cluster’s demand by up to 40% and followed reduction
requests lasting up to 10 h [4]. Much of an AI fleet’s work
can be paused, capped or deferred [5], and an operator with
several sites can also move it [6].
Turning this potential into grid value requires a model that
connects the operator’s controls to the grid. On the data-center
side, the controls act on individual GPUs and jobs: a power
cap trades throughput for power, training can pause and resume
from checkpoints, offline jobs have deadlines, and inference
must meet response-time targets. On the grid side, what
matters is each site’s facility power, including cooling, and the
locational prices and market rules it faces. Geographic load
balancing [6] and carbon-aware scheduling [5] move work
between sites and over time, respectively, but do not model
GPU power caps. Grid studies, conversely, typically assume
that a fixed share of data-center load can be deferred [7], [8];
a trace of 155,410 GPUs instead derived flexibility from the
workloads eligible to curtail and found that it averages about
6% of facility power [9].
Such a model must also be clear about where savings come
from. An AI fleet that faces electricity prices can lower its
bill in three ways. It can run GPUs at lower power caps,
which finishes the same work with less energy at any price.
It can shift work in time, toward hours when power is cheap.
And it can move work between sites, toward whichever site
has cheaper power at that moment. Only the last two respond
to prices, yet all three appear as savings when an optimized
schedule is compared with a fleet that runs every job at full
power on arrival, which counts efficiency as flexibility.
This paper makes the following contributions:
1) A scheduling framework for a multi-site AI data-center
fleet that links GPU power-cap levels and workload con-
straints to site facility power and locational electricity
prices. It is a linear program that sets each site’s hourly
power a day ahead from day-ahead (DA) prices.
2) A year-long demonstration on 2025 CAISO DA prices
in three data-center markets. Four operating modes, each
adding one capability, split the saving into efficiency,
price response in time and routing between sites, with
confidence intervals. Coordinated scheduling saves 6.3%
at equal work; efficiency and price response carry nearly
all of it, and routing adds a small share, mainly on days
when prices at the sites diverge.
Because the framework ties GPU-level controls to grid-facing
quantities, it provides a basis for valuing data-center grid
services such as demand response and reserves.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II
models the fleet and its operating modes. Section III describes
the simulation setup, Section IV presents the results, and
Section V concludes this work.
II. FLEET SCHEDULING MODEL
A data center fleet operator manages a fleet of data centers
over time windows of length ∆indexed by t, so that the t-th
time window corresponds to the time interval [(t −1)∆, t∆].
Each data center i hosts Ni identical GPUs. The fleet operator
sets for every time interval 1) how many GPUs are assigned
to each computational job, 2) at which power cap the GPUs
run, and, 3) when sites are coordinated, to which site movable
work is transferred.
We assume for simplicity that the fleet is a price taker,
i.e., the fleet operator schedules against locational marginal
prices (LMPs) which are not affected by the data center loads.
We will cast the fleet operator scheduling program as a linear
program (LP), which can be efficiently solved by off the shelf
methods, with continuous decision variables. The formulation
follows geographic load balancing [6], with per-job deadlines
in place of the daily completion window of [5].
We assume two types of work here. Deferrable jobs, indexed
by m, must finish by a deadline but may be paused, slowed
and, in some cases, moved to other sites. They range from
training runs that last weeks, use thousands of GPUs and
are pinned to their site, to short jobs such as fine-tuning,
evaluation and data processing that last hours and may run at

In the following, Sections II-A–II-E build the LP; Sec-
tion II-F describes the day ahead (DA) schedule and the four
operating modes we compare. Fig. 1 shows how the pieces fit
together at one site, and Table I summarizes the notation.
A. GPU Power Levels
Power capping [10] lets a GPU run at a few discrete levels
k, which depend on its workload class. A GPU assigned to
job m at level k draws a fraction ϕm,k of its thermal design
power (TDP) and has corresponding relative throughput rm,k:
one hour at level k completes rm,k GPU-hours of uncapped
work. The last level K is the natural, uncapped draw, with
rm,K = 1. We assume a GPU can also split a step between
two levels; it then averages their power and throughput and
operates on the straight line between them; see the inset of
Fig. 1. Throughput is therefore a piecewise-linear function of
power. The levels show diminishing returns: each extra watt
buys less throughput, so this function is concave. This allows
us to trade off GPU throughput for power saving, especially
in presence of flexible job deadlines. We define nm,i,t,k as the
number of GPUs allocated to job m at site i and time interval
t capped at the power level k. For simplicity, we consider
nm,i,t,k as a continuous rather than discrete variable, given
the big number of GPUs (tens of thousands) in each site.
B. Deferrable Jobs
Deferrable jobs are measured in GPU-hours (GPU-h) at un-
capped throughput: W = 1,000 GPU-h keeps 1,000 uncapped
GPUs busy for one hour, or 1,000 GPUs at rm,k = 0.5 for
two hours. A deferrable job m that arrives is characterized
by its work Wm and by the maximum number of GPUs that
may be allocated to it at once Gm. To each site i, the schedule
assigns a share ym,i of job m, with P
i ym,i = 1, and allocates
nm,i,t,k GPUs at level k. Usually, training runs are pinned to
their home site im, short jobs are more easily moved. After
job m started to be processed in site i, the remaining work
left at time t is denoted as wm,i,t and evolves like an account
balance (the tank in Fig. 1) over the planning horizon, which
ends at step H:
wm,i,t+1 = wm,i,t −∆P
k rm,knm,i,t,k +δum,i,t,
(1a)
um,i,t = max{P
k(nm,i,t,k −nm,i,t−1,k), 0},
(1b)
wm,i,am = Wm ym,i,
(1c)
P
k nm,i,t,k ≤Gm ym,i,
(1d)
wm,i,H ≤Wm ym,i max{dm −H, 0}/(dm −am),
(1e)
where um,i,t is the GPUs of job m that start up in step t,
and am and dm are the arrival step and deadline of job m.
Equation (1a) updates the remaining work by subtracting the
work GPUs complete and by adding the cost of restarting
GPUs: a GPU that resumes a paused job must reload the last
checkpoint and redo the work done after last saving, so it
spends δ hours busy without progress. Equation (1b) counts
the GPUs that start up: the increase in running GPUs. The LP
imposes (1b) linearly as um,i,t ≥P
k(nm,i,t,k −nm,i,t−1,k)
and um,i,t ≥0: since restarts only add work, um,i,t meets this
bound at the optimum. Constraints (1c) and (1d) give site i its
share of the job’s work and of its GPU limit. Constraint (1e)
is a pace limit: the work left at the end of the horizon may
not exceed a straight-line path to the deadline. A training run
due in 10 days must finish at least 10% of its work on the
first day, and a short job due within the horizon must finish
completely.
C. Online Inference
Inference is live traffic and cannot be delayed, so it has no
work balance. The demand arising at site j, Qj,t, is measured
in GPU-equivalents, the number of uncapped GPUs it would
fully occupy during the time slot t. A part qj,i,t of it is
served at site i by ninf,i,t,k inference GPUs at level k. At this
DA planning stage, we assume the serving GPUs are loaded
to at most a fraction ¯ρ of their capacity, the same at every
site, which leaves slack for bursts of requests [6], [11]. The
inference constraints are:
P
i qj,i,t = Qj,t,
(2a)
¯ρ P
k rinf,kninf,i,t,k ≥P
j qj,i,t,
(2b)
P
m,k nm,i,t,k ≤Ni.
(2c)
Constraint (2a) serves all inference demand, (2b) gives each
site enough serving GPUs for the demand it takes at utilization
¯ρ, and (2c) keeps all GPUs in use (including deferrable jobs
and inference) within the Ni GPUs of the site. In fleet mode
demand may be served at any site; otherwise qj,i,t = 0 for
i̸ = j. With ¯ρ = 0.8, serving 1,000 GPU-equivalents takes
1,250 uncapped GPUs, or 1,543 at 46% of TDP. The lower
cap may need more GPUs but less power overall.

Every GPU slot, with its share of the server, draws pidle

E. Objective and Optimization Problem
The goal for the operator is to minimize the following
objective function:
J = P

where λi,t, πlate, and πroute are price for electricity, lateness,
and inference routing. The first term captures the energy bill,
the second term models a late penalty πlate on each GPU-hour
of work still unfinished after its deadline, the third term sums
the value of the work left at the end of the horizon, which
must still be done later, the fourth term is the cost of moving
a job’s data away from its home site, and the fifth term is a
small routing cost for serving inference away from where it
arises. Here, the leftover work is valued at:
vm = pm,K PUE ¯λ + κ,
(6)
where the first term is the energy needed to finish the work
later, at this day’s mean price ¯λ, and the second, κ in $/GPU-
h, is the value of the GPU time the work will occupy, since a
GPU-hour deferred today displaces other work later. The two
differ greatly in scale: at $39/MWh, the energy of a training
GPU-hour costs about $0.03, while an H100 GPU rents for
about $2/h. $2/h is near the rental value, so training is never
deferred, consistent with [9], and every mode completes the
same work.
We can now cast our scheduling problem as the LP:

(7b)

(7c)
with ym,im = 1 for training runs and in the site-level modes.
The LP input parameters are the prices λ, the workload
(Wm, Qj,t) and the starting state; its outputs are the GPU
counts per level, the placement and the facility power at
each site. To keep the LP always feasible, the implementation
softens the pace limit (1e) and the inference balance (2a) with
penalties of $20/GPU-h and $5,000 per GPU-equivalent-hour;
neither is incurred in the simulation results.
F. DA Schedule and Operating Modes
The fleet schedules each operating day in CAISO’s DA
market. The LP is solved once, in hourly steps (∆= 1h)
over the 24 hours of the day, with the DA LMPs λi,t and
the day’s workload. Its hourly power Pi,t is the fleet’s DA
purchase, which it then consumes as scheduled, so its bill is
the first term of (5), P
i,t λi,tPi,t∆.
We compare four modes. Each adds one capability to the
one before it, so that the difference between consecutive modes
isolates one source of saving:

1) Uncoordinated: every job runs on arrival at its home
site at full power, inference first, then training runs, then
short jobs in arrival order.
2) Price-blind: the site-level model is solved at a flat price,
with a negligible preference for early work. This isolates
operational efficiency.
3) Site-level: the model is solved on LMPs, with all work
and inference kept at its home site.
4) Fleet-coordinated: the model is solved on LMPs and
also optimizes routing (y and q).
All modes pay the DA LMPs for the power they draw. Thus
(b) minus (a) measures efficiency, (c) minus (b) measures price
response in time, and (d) minus (c) measures routing.
III. SIMULATION SETUP
A. Fleet and Prices
Three sites host 210,000 GPUs in total. When run uncoordi-
nated, they average about 190 MW with a mean daily peak of
230 MW. The sites are placed in CAISO’s three largest data-
center markets, Silicon Valley, the Los Angeles basin and San
Diego. Each site pays the LMP that CAISO publishes for its
local area (PG&E South Bay, SCE Core and SDG&E).
The 2025 hourly DA LMPs come from CAISO’s OA-
SIS data portal [14]. DA prices at the three sites averaged
$39/MWh and peaked at $199/MWh, and midday solar output
drove them below zero at some site on 102 days. Silicon
Valley was the most expensive market, with an average price
of $43/MWh against $35/MWh in Los Angeles.
B. Workload and Runs
We assume each site runs two training runs on 26% of its
GPUs, with 5–30 days left to run and a 15% deadline slack.
These runs are pinned to their cluster, as large synchronous
runs are. Short jobs arrive following a business-day profile,
totaling 19% of GPU capacity per day with lognormal volume,
and may move between sites; those arriving in the same 3-h
window with the same deadline are modeled as one job. Each
short job is due 6, 12 or 24 h after arrival, with assumed
probabilities 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5, within the 24-h window. Online

inference follows a diurnal shape with an assumed peak-to-
trough ratio of 1.6 for the fleet’s mix of services. Average
GPU allocation is about 75%.
The workload is taken as known a day ahead. Each day
is simulated from a fresh state with an independent workload
draw, and training runs enter at a random point in their run.
Every day of 2025 (365 days) is simulated in all four modes.
Models are built in Pyomo and solved with HiGHS.
IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
A. Efficiency, Price Response and Routing
Table III summarizes the year. All modes complete the
same 835 million GPU-hours of deferrable work, serve all
inference demand and finish every short job by its deadline,
so the comparison is at equal output. Fleet coordination cuts
energy cost by 6.3%, or about $4.1M per year and $2.5/MWh
consumed. Taking differences between consecutive modes
splits this saving into three parts, each in percentage points
of the uncoordinated cost; Fig. 2(a) shows them by month.
Efficiency: 3.8%. Run at a flat price, the optimizer spreads
work across spare GPUs at lower power caps, cutting energy
by 4.7% and the mean daily peak by 16%. The gain comes
from inference and short jobs. At 46% of TDP, a GPU runs
each inference request about 1.2 times slower but draws much
less power. For training, the gain is under 1%: its runs already
use their full GPU limit, so a lower cap would only slow them.
Price response: 2.3%. Responding to LMPs lowers the
average price paid by 3.6% relative to the price-blind schedule,
mainly by moving work into the midday hours, when solar
output lowers prices (Fig. 2(b)). Its value follows the solar
season: about 7% in March and April, when midday prices
fell below zero on most days, but only about 1% from July to
September.
Routing: 0.2%. It exceeds 1% on 23 days. On April 7
(Fig. 2(c)), for example, midday DA prices fell below zero in
Los Angeles and San Diego but averaged $25/MWh in Silicon
Valley. The fleet mode moved about 6 MW of midday load
out of Silicon Valley, which was worth 2.1% that day.
V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This paper developed a modelling and simulation framework
that links an AI data-center fleet’s GPU power caps, job
timing and job placement to site power and locational prices.
Formulated as a linear program, it remains tractable at fleet
scale, and nested scenarios that release one degree of freedom
at a time separate efficiency from price-responsive flexibility.

Fig. 2. Results over 2025. (a) Monthly fleet saving relative to the uncoordinated mode. (b) Average day: fleet power by mode and DA LMP by site, averaged
over all days for each hour; the site-level and fleet curves nearly coincide. (c) April 7: the price-responsive modes fill the negative-price solar hours, and the
fleet mode also moves load out of Silicon Valley.
On 2025 CAISO day-ahead prices, coordinated scheduling
lowers energy cost by 6.3% at equal work: 3.8% from price-
independent power-cap efficiency, 2.3% from temporal shifting
and 0.2% from spatial routing. Routing gains little within one
ISO, where nodal prices are strongly correlated, but should be
worth more across sites with larger price differences, such as
congested nodes or different ISOs.
Ongoing work will add real-time operation, re-solving the
LP every 15 min by model-predictive control on CAISO’s
fifteen-minute market prices, accounting for prediction errors
and uncertainties. Future work will use the model to schedule
and value grid services such as demand response, voltage and
frequency regulation, and couple it with the network through
congestion-aware allocation and AC optimal power flow.
